clue.text: Deceive lover - in light from this?

definitions.note: The definition is a description rather than a synonym: a flambeau is the thing light comes from, and the question mark flags the roundabout phrasing.

blocks.note: To flam is an old word for to trick or deceive, as in flim-flam.
A beau is a boyfriend or suitor.

explanation.surface: Someone warns that a lover might deceive you when seen in a flattering light.
explanation.walkthrough: FLAM survives mostly in 'flim-flam' and in crosswords, so it is worth owning. The question mark admits that 'light from this' describes the answer rather than naming it.
explanation.definitionFit: A flambeau is a flaming torch, so it is literally a source of light; the clue defines it by what it gives off.

clue.text: Mistake following trip, after leaving Thailand

indicators.note: Something that has left is no longer there.

blocks.note: F is the standard abbreviation for 'following', as in 'p. 12 f.'
A trip and a tumble are both falls.
T is Thailand's international vehicle registration letter, removed from TUMBLE to leave UMBLE.

explanation.surface: A traveller makes a blunder just after flying out of Thailand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trip' reads as a holiday in the surface, but it is the stumble kind. Thailand is only the single letter T on a car's country plate.
explanation.definitionFit: To fumble is to handle something clumsily and get it wrong, so it is a plain synonym for making a mistake.

clue.text: Kitchen ingredient a pointer to grub

blocks.note: An arrow on a sign is a pointer.
To grub is to dig or root about in the soil.

explanation.surface: A cookery tip: this ingredient points you towards food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grub' is food in the surface and a verb in the wordplay: to grub and to root are both to dig around.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrowroot is a starch powder used in kitchens to thicken sauces, so it is a specific example of a kitchen ingredient.

clue.text: Unhappy over broadcaster’s description of innovative thinking?

indicators.note: In a down clue the word placed over another is written above it, so this piece comes first.

blocks.note: Feeling blue is feeling sad.
Sky is a British satellite broadcaster.

explanation.surface: A gloomy television company describes its fresh thinking.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's reads as a possessive but is really 'is', joining the wordplay to the definition. The question mark flags that the definition describes how the answer is used rather than naming it.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue-sky thinking is open, unconstrained, creative thought, so the adjective is exactly the one applied to innovative thinking.

clue.text: Deep area at the side of ship

blocks.note: A is a standard abbreviation for area.
Standing by something is standing beside it.
SS stands for steamship, the prefix on ships' names.

explanation.surface: A deep stretch of water alongside a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deep' looks like an adjective describing the area, but it is the noun, as in 'the deep' for the ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: An abyss is a bottomless depth, and 'the deep' as a noun means just such a profound gulf or sea.

clue.text: Harry Potter actor performed? About time

indicators.note: Something about another thing goes round it.

blocks.note: An actor who performed was on, as in on stage.
T is the standard abbreviation for time.

explanation.surface: A question about whether a Harry Potter actor has played the part, and a remark that it was about time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About time' reads as an exclamation of impatience, but it is an instruction to put T inside. 'Performed' needs two words, WAS ON, as in being on stage.
explanation.definitionFit: Emma Watson played Hermione Granger in the Harry Potter films, so she is a specific instance of the actor named.

clue.text: Surrounding temperature supports the last word about peaks in British Isles

indicators.note: In a down clue the supporting piece sits underneath.
Something about another goes round it.
Peaks are the tops of things.

blocks.note: Amen is the word said at the end of a prayer.
The first letters of British and Isles.
T is the standard abbreviation for temperature.

explanation.surface: A weather report on the temperature around mountain tops in Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ambient temperature' is a real phrase, so the surface hands you the collocation to distract from the definition. 'The last word' is AMEN, the word that closes a prayer.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambient describes the conditions all around you, as in ambient noise, so it is a plain synonym for surrounding.

clue.text: Poster endorses rising car brand

indicators.note: In a down clue a rising word is read from the bottom up, so the letters come out backwards.

blocks.note: An ad on a wall is a poster.
To OK something is to approve or endorse it.

explanation.surface: A billboard backs an up-and-coming car maker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poster' tempts you to think of someone who posts; it is the advertisement itself. 'Rising' in a surface about business sounds like success.
explanation.definitionFit: Skoda is a Czech car manufacturer, so it is a specific example of a car brand.

clue.text: Studying disease? Never alone, generally discontented

indicators.note: A word with no content has lost its middle, leaving only its outside letters.

blocks.note: No as in 'no way', a flat never.
Doing something solo is doing it alone.
The outer letters of GENERALLY.

explanation.surface: Someone researching illness finds that people are never alone and usually unhappy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discontented' reads as unhappy, but it is an instruction to empty a word of its contents. The question mark flags that the definition is a description of the discipline.
explanation.definitionFit: Nosology is the branch of medicine that classifies diseases, so studying disease describes what practitioners of it do.

clue.text: Very happy to secure copper or another metal

indicators.note: To secure something is to hold it fast, so the outer word holds the metal symbol inside.

blocks.note: Merry means jolly and happy.
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper.

explanation.surface: A cheerful metalworker who has got hold of some copper or some other metal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another' ties the definition to copper: the answer is a second metal, not the first one mentioned. Cu comes from the Latin cuprum.
explanation.definitionFit: Mercury is a metallic element, liquid at room temperature, so it is a metal other than the copper already named.

clue.text: Generous, holding back –then old will board vehicle that’s almost full

indicators.note: Held back means turned the other way.

blocks.note: Generous, as in a big helping, is BIG, reversed to GIB.
A bus is a vehicle.
O is a standard abbreviation for old.

explanation.surface: A mean-spirited passenger, then an elderly one, getting on a nearly full bus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost full' in the surface describes the crowded vehicle, but it defines the moon's phase. BIG for generous, as in a big-hearted gift.
explanation.definitionFit: A gibbous moon is more than half lit but less than full, so the astronomer's word means exactly almost full.

clue.text: Film composer’s significant success

blocks.note: A good sum is a significant, sizeable one.
A win is a success.

explanation.surface: A movie composer has a big hit.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is', joining the composer to his wordplay. GOOD has its sense of sizeable, as in 'a good distance'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ron Goodwin wrote scores for films such as 633 Squadron and Where Eagles Dare, so he is a specific example of a film composer.

clue.text: British author showing some simple wisdom

indicators.note: Some of something is only a part of it, so the answer is a stretch of the following words.

blocks.note: Hidden in simpLE WISdom.

explanation.surface: A British writer displays a bit of plain good sense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Showing' is doing double duty in the surface as displaying, but in the wordplay it just joins definition to the hidden letters.
explanation.definitionFit: C.S. Lewis, author of the Narnia books, was a British writer, so he is a specific example of the definition.

clue.text: Booth blocked by single week’s delay

indicators.note: Something blocked by another has it stuck inside.

blocks.note: A market stall is a booth.
Single means one.
W is the standard abbreviation for week.

explanation.surface: A market stall is held up by a week's hold-up.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is' linking the wordplay to the definition, not a possessive. The definition sits at the end, disguised as part of the week.
explanation.definitionFit: To stonewall is to stall by obstruction and evasion, as in cricket blocking or a politician refusing to answer, so it means to delay.

clue.text: Horse backed in some difficulty - no pressure

indicators.note: To back is to go in reverse, so the hidden letters are read backwards.
Something in some words is inside part of them, so the answer lies hidden in the text.

blocks.note: Hidden backwards in difficultY NO Pressure.

explanation.surface: A horse bet on in a tough race, with nothing riding on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backed' reads as a racing bet, but it reverses the hidden letters. They straddle three words, including the hyphen that the eye skips.
explanation.definitionFit: A pony is a small horse, so the answer is a kind of horse.

clue.text: Front line of horses - it may be drawn going into battle

definitions.text: it may be drawn going into battle

blocks.note: The bow is the front of a ship.
A trainer's string is the line of racehorses in his stable.

explanation.surface: Cavalry lined up at the front, one thing pulled out as they charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawn' suggests a sword, which fits a cavalry charge; an archer draws a string back instead. A string of horses is the racing term for a stable's runners.
explanation.definitionFit: An archer draws the bowstring back before loosing an arrow, so it is described by what happens to it on a battlefield.

clue.text: Objection over resonant sound from part of posterior?

indicators.note: In a down clue the word placed over another is written above it.

blocks.note: 'But' is an objection, as in 'no ifs or buts'.
Tock is the deeper second beat of a clock's tick-tock.

explanation.surface: Someone objects to an echoing noise coming out of a backside.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points at a rude noise, but the sound is a clock's. The question mark signals the playful definition of one cheek of the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: The posterior is the bottom, and each of its two halves is a buttock, so a buttock is literally part of the posterior.

clue.text: Partying males keeping from occupying popular male territory?

indicators.note: Letters that are partying are dancing about, so the word's letters are rearranged.
To keep something is to hold it, so the rearranged letters hold the next word inside.
To occupy a place is to be inside it.

blocks.note: Something in fashion is popular.
MALES rearranged, split around the next piece.
Made of something is made from it.

explanation.surface: A gang of revellers sets up camp in a men-only party zone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Male territory' sounds like a stag-party venue; it is the island named Man. 'From' giving OF is the made-of sense, as in a statue made from bronze.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man is a self-governing British Crown dependency, and the question mark flags the pun of its name as the territory belonging to Man.

clue.text: Delight over line adopted by youngster in choir

indicators.note: In a down clue the word placed over another is written above it.

blocks.note: Glee is delight.
A cub is a young animal, and a junior scout.
L is the standard abbreviation for line.

explanation.surface: A joyful solo line given to the child in the choir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Line' sounds like a sung phrase in the choir surface, but it is only the letter L. A glee is also an unaccompanied part-song, which is where the club got its name.
explanation.definitionFit: A glee club is a singing society, originally for glees, so it is a kind of choir.

clue.text: London theatre sounding unimportant and not revolutionary

indicators.note: Sounding like something is being heard as it.
A revolution is a full turn, so a word that is revolutionary is turned round.

blocks.note: Something little is small and unimportant.
NOT turned round.

explanation.surface: A London theatre that sounds minor and has no radical ambitions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not revolutionary' reads as tame politics, but the 'not' is the letters to spin. The Lyttelton is one of the three stages of the National Theatre on the South Bank.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lyttelton is one of the National Theatre's auditoria in London, named after its first chairman, so it is a specific London theatre.

clue.text: Impress English with excellent review

blocks.note: Eng is the standard abbreviation for English.
A rave is a glowing review.

explanation.surface: An English critic's enthusiastic notice makes an impression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Impress' pushes you towards being admired, but here it means pressing a mark into a surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To engrave is to cut a design into a surface, and to impress is likewise to stamp a mark into something.

clue.text: Pointless isolated life, empty

indicators.note: An empty word has lost its insides, leaving only its first and last letters.

blocks.note: The outer letters of ISOLATED.
The outer letters of LIFE.

explanation.surface: A lament for a lonely, meaningless, hollow existence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Empty' looks like another adjective in a gloomy list, but it tells you to empty both words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Idle can mean futile or groundless, as in idle threats or idle speculation, so it matches pointless.

clue.text: Assume I note sex appeal surrounding that woman

indicators.note: Surrounding something means going all round it.

blocks.note: I stands as itself.
N is an abbreviation for note.
Her is the pronoun for that woman.
'It' is old slang for sex appeal, from the 1927 film 'It' starring Clara Bow.

explanation.surface: A man presumes that a certain woman is attractive.
explanation.walkthrough: IT for sex appeal is a crossword staple from the 1920s, when the 'It girl' had it. 'Assume' reads as presume, but it means take on.
explanation.definitionFit: To assume a role or debt is to take it on, which is what you do when you inherit it from a predecessor.

clue.text: Hesitates to deceive group of scientists

blocks.note: To have someone is to trick them, as in 'you've been had'.
RS is the Royal Society, Britain's academy of scientists.

explanation.surface: A person dithers over whether to hoodwink a panel of researchers.
explanation.walkthrough: HAVE in the sense of 'you've been had' is the key; 'to' belongs with it. Haver is mainly British and Scottish usage for dithering.
explanation.definitionFit: To haver is to dither or vacillate, a chiefly British use, so havers is a straight synonym for hesitates.

clue.text: Outrageous for one of the monarchs to claim Ohio

indicators.note: To claim something is to take hold of it, so the royal word takes the state letter inside.

blocks.note: E.g. means for example, or 'for one'.
Regius is Latin for royal, belonging to the monarch, as in a Regius professor.
O was the traditional abbreviation for Ohio before the two-letter postal codes.

explanation.surface: An outrage that a royal should lay claim to an American state.
explanation.walkthrough: A Regius professorship is a chair founded by the Crown, which is where REGIUS turns up in English. 'For one' is the example-marker E.G.
explanation.definitionFit: Egregious means shockingly bad, as in an egregious error, so it is a plain synonym for outrageous.

clue.text: German river locally flowing in here? Not entirely

indicators.note: Letters that are flowing move about freely, so they are rearranged.
Not the entire thing means one letter short, so the last letter drops off.

blocks.note: The two words taken as letters.

explanation.surface: A question whether the German river runs through this place, answered with a partial yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Locally' means the name as the Germans spell it, not the English Rhine. 'Flowing' suits a river in the surface and scrambles the letters in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhein is the German spelling of the Rhine, so it is what the river is called locally.

clue.text: Prophet cycling over a Pacific location

indicators.note: Cycling goes round in a loop, so the last letter comes round to the front.
In a down clue the word placed over another is written above it.

blocks.note: AMOS, the Old Testament prophet, with his final S moved to the front.
A stands as itself.

explanation.surface: A prophet biking across a spot in the Pacific.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' conjures a bicycle, but it moves the end letter to the start. Amos is one of the short-named minor prophets crosswords use often.
explanation.definitionFit: Samoa is an island nation in the South Pacific, so it is a specific Pacific location.

clue.text: Additional oxygen blended with H2O leading to a fuss

indicators.note: Blended things are mixed together, so the letters are rearranged.
Something leading to another goes in front of it, so the mixed letters come before the rest.

blocks.note: O is the chemical symbol for oxygen, and 'additional' means one more.
The formula for water spelt out: two H's and an O.
A stands as itself.

explanation.surface: A chemistry demonstration, adding extra oxygen to water, ends in uproar.
explanation.walkthrough: H2O has to be read as its letters HHO. Extra oxygen makes hydrogen peroxide, which is the chemistry the surface nods at.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoo-ha is a commotion or fuss, an informal British word, so it is a straight synonym.

clue.text: Misinformation returned? Don’t worry

blocks.note: A lie is false information.
Someone returned is back.

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a false story has come round again, and is told not to fret.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returned' tempts you to reverse something, but it is simply BACK, as in 'she's back'.
explanation.definitionFit: Told to lie back, you relax and stop fretting, so the imperative idiom matches don't worry.

clue.text: Sea at Calais that is enthralling the writer, French writer

indicators.note: To enthral is to hold captive.

blocks.note: Mer is French for sea, and Calais tells you to think in French.
I.e. abbreviates id est, that is.
The writer of the clue refers to himself as ME.

explanation.surface: A French author gazes spellbound at the sea off Calais.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The writer' is the setter himself, ME, while 'French writer' is the answer. Prosper Mérimée wrote the novella Carmen that Bizet turned into an opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Prosper Mérimée was a nineteenth-century French novelist and dramatist, so he is a specific example of a French writer.

clue.text: Fictional schoolboy: with more candour, no learner

blocks.note: Blunt speech is candid, so more candid is blunter.
L is for learner, as on British learner-driver plates, removed from BLUNTER.

explanation.surface: A storybook pupil who speaks more frankly and has no student driver with him.
explanation.walkthrough: Billy Bunter is the greedy 'Fat Owl' of Greyfriars School in Frank Richards's stories. L for learner comes from the L-plates on British learner cars.
explanation.definitionFit: Billy Bunter is the famous schoolboy of Frank Richards's Greyfriars stories, so he is a specific fictional schoolboy.

clue.text: Scene of battle keeps retaining sharpness

indicators.note: To retain something is to hold it in, so the first word holds the second inside.

blocks.note: To have something is to keep it.
Sting is sharpness, as in the sting of a remark.

explanation.surface: A castle's keeps still have their sharp edge, a battlefield scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keeps' reads as a castle tower in a battle surface, but it is the verb HAS. The Battle of Hastings in 1066 is the one every English schoolchild knows.
explanation.definitionFit: Hastings is the English town near which William of Normandy defeated Harold in 1066, so it is a famous scene of battle.
